title: RC charging and time constant
text:
For a resistor and capacitor in series, the time constant sets the pace of charging and discharging:
\[
\tau = RC
\]
After one time constant, a charging capacitor reaches about 63.2% of its final value; after five, it’s considered fully settled (99.3%).

title: RC charging and time constant
text:
For a resistor and capacitor in series, the time constant sets the pace of charging and discharging:
\[
\tau = RC
\]
After one time constant, a charging capacitor reaches about 63.2% of its final value; after five, it’s considered fully settled (99.3%).

title: RC charging and time constant
text:
Charging from zero
Starting from 0 V toward a supply \(V_s\):
\[
V(t) = V_s \left(1 - e^{-t/\tau}\right)
\]
Discharging back toward 0 V from \(V_s\) follows the mirror image, \(V(t) = V_s e^{-t/\tau}\).

title: Ohm’s law and power
text: The relationship every other circuit identity gets built on top of.

title: Ohm’s law and power
text:
The law
For a resistor, voltage and current are proportional:
\[
V = IR
\]
Power dissipated follows from \(P = VI\), substituted with Ohm’s law to give two more useful forms:
\[
P = VI = I^2 R = \frac{V^2}{R}
\]
The \(I^2R\) form is the one that matters for sizing: double the current through a fixed resistance and dissipation quadruples, not doubles — a common reason parts run hotter than expected after a “small” current increase.

title: Ohm’s law and power
text:
Calculator
Enter a supply voltage and resistance to get current and dissipated power.

title: Voltage divider
text:
Two resistors in series across a supply split the voltage in proportion to resistance:
\[
V_{out} = V_{in} \cdot \frac{R_2}{R_1 + R_2}
\]

title: Voltage divider
text:
Two resistors in series across a supply split the voltage in proportion to resistance:
\[
V_{out} = V_{in} \cdot \frac{R_2}{R_1 + R_2}
\]

title: Voltage divider
text:
Loaded divider
Once something draws current from the output node — an ADC input, another circuit — that load resistor \(R_L\) sits in parallel with \(R_2\), and the divider ratio changes:
\[
V_{out} = V_{in} \cdot \frac{R_2 \| R_L}{R_1 + (R_2 \| R_L)}, \qquad R_2 \| R_L = \frac{R_2 R_L}{R_2 + R_L}
\]
This is why a divider that measures correctly open-circuit can read low once connected to a real load — the rule of thumb is to keep \(R_L \gg R_2\), typically 10× or more.

title: Boost converter
text: A boost converter steps a DC input up to a higher DC output by storing energy in an inductor while a switch is closed, then dumping it into the output (through a diode or synchronous switch) once it opens. Ideal CCM analysis again.

title: Boost converter
text:
Duty cycle
\[
D = 1 - \frac{V_{in}}{V_{out}}
\]

title: Boost converter
text:
Inductor current
While the switch is on, the full input voltage sits across the inductor, so ripple current is:
\[
\Delta I_L = \frac{V_{in} D}{f_{sw} L} \quad \Rightarrow \quad L = \frac{V_{in} D}{f_{sw}\, \Delta I_L}
\]
Unlike a buck, the inductor carries the input current, not the output current — this is why boost converters need bulkier inductors for the same output power. By power balance (\(V_{in}I_{in} = V_{out}I_{out}\), ideal):
\[
I_{L,avg} = I_{in} = \frac{I_{out}}{1-D}
\]

title: Buck converter
text: A buck converter steps a DC input down to a lower DC output by switching an inductor between the input and ground, then filtering the result. This is the ideal, continuous-conduction-mode (CCM) analysis — enough to pick a starting inductor and output capacitor.

title: Buck converter
text:
Duty cycle
Ignoring losses, the output is set entirely by duty cycle:
\[
D = \frac{V_{out}}{V_{in}}
\]

title: Buck converter
text:
Inductor selection
While the switch is on, the inductor sees \((V_{in} - V_{out})\) across it for time \(D/f_{sw}\); while off, it sees \(-V_{out}\) for \((1-D)/f_{sw}\). Either way gives the same ripple current:
\[
\Delta I_L = \frac{V_{out}(1 - D)}{f_{sw} L}
\]
Solving for \(L\) at a target ripple (commonly 20–40% of \(I_{out}\)):
\[
L = \frac{V_{out}(1-D)}{f_{sw}\, \Delta I_L}
\]

title: Buck converter
text:
Output capacitor
Assuming the ripple is dominated by capacitance (not ESR), the output voltage ripple is approximately:
\[
\Delta V_{out} \approx \frac{\Delta I_L}{8\, f_{sw}\, C_{out}} \quad \Rightarrow \quad C_{out} = \frac{\Delta I_L}{8\, f_{sw}\, \Delta V_{out}}
\]
Real capacitors also add ESR-driven ripple (\(\Delta V_{ESR} = \Delta I_L \cdot R_{ESR}\)) on top of this — worth checking separately against the datasheet ESR once a part is chosen.

title: Single-layer air-core solenoid: inductance
text: A quick derivation of solenoid inductance from first principles, then the practical correction engineers actually use, with a calculator to try real turn counts and dimensions.

title: Single-layer air-core solenoid: inductance
text:
The ideal case
Treating the coil as infinitely long, Ampere’s law gives a uniform field inside: \(B = \mu_0 n I\), where \(n = N / l\) is turns per unit length. Flux linkage through all \(N\) turns gives:
\[
L_{ideal} = \mu_0 N^2 \frac{\pi r^2}{l}
\]
This overestimates inductance for any real, finite coil — it ignores fringing at the ends.



Fig. 1 — field concentrated inside the winding, with fringing paths returning outside.

title: Single-layer air-core solenoid: inductance
text:
Wheeler’s correction
For a real single-layer coil where length isn’t much greater than radius, Wheeler’s 1928 approximation is the standard practical formula (\(r\), \(l\) in inches, result in \(\mu H\)):
\[
L_{\mu H} \approx \frac{r^2 N^2}{9r + 10l}
\]
Valid roughly for \(l > 0.4r\). Below that, it undercorrects and a full Nagaoka-coefficient treatment is needed.



Fig. 2 — field strength rising with current, fringing appearing at the ends.

text:
Sends a local file as raw bytes over a Web Serial connection, with a progress bar. This is the useful 10% of a “programmer” that’s generic across hardware: getting bytes out the USB port reliably. It does not implement any chip-specific flashing protocol (STK500, avrdude’s protocols, DFU, ESP32’s ROM bootloader handshake, and so on) — those are stateful protocols with their own framing and handshakes, specific to each target. What this covers is the common case underneath: a simple UART bootloader that just wants the raw image streamed in, or any other device where you need to push a known byte sequence out a serial port from the browser.

title: Op-amp basics and example circuits
text: An operational amplifier is a high-gain differential amplifier IC: two inputs, one output, and an open-loop gain so large (typically 100,000 to over 1,000,000) that it’s almost never used open-loop. Nearly every real op-amp circuit wraps it in negative feedback — a resistor network feeding some of the output back to the inverting input — which trades away that enormous raw gain for precision, stability, and a gain set by resistors instead of by the (loosely specified, temperature-dependent) op-amp itself.

title: Op-amp basics and example circuits
text:
The two golden rules
For an ideal op-amp in a negative-feedback configuration:

No current flows into either input. Input impedance is effectively infinite.
The output does whatever it takes to force the two inputs to the same voltage — a “virtual short,” not an actual electrical connection, and it only holds while the feedback loop is active and the output isn’t saturated against a supply rail.

Everything below follows from just those two rules plus Ohm’s law and KCL.

title: Op-amp basics and example circuits
text:
Non-inverting amplifier
The input goes straight to the non-inverting terminal; feedback resistor \(R_f\) and ground resistor \(R_{in}\) form a divider from output back to the inverting terminal.
By rule 2, \(V_- = V_+ = V_{in}\). \(V_-\) is also set by the feedback divider: \(V_- = V_{out}\frac{R_{in}}{R_{in}+R_f}\). Setting these equal and solving for \(V_{out}/V_{in}\):
\[
A_v = \frac{V_{out}}{V_{in}} = 1 + \frac{R_f}{R_{in}}
\]
Gain is always \(\geq 1\), output is in phase with the input, and input impedance is very high (the op-amp’s own input impedance) — this is the configuration to reach for when the source can’t tolerate being loaded down.

title: Op-amp basics and example circuits
text:
Inverting amplifier
The input drives \(R_{in}\) into the inverting terminal; the non-inverting terminal ties to ground; \(R_f\) feeds back from output to the same inverting node.
By rule 2, \(V_- = V_+ = 0\) — a “virtual ground,” even though nothing is physically tied to ground there. By rule 1, all the current through \(R_{in}\) must continue through \(R_f\) (none can go into the op-amp input):
\[
\frac{V_{in} - 0}{R_{in}} = \frac{0 - V_{out}}{R_f} \quad \Rightarrow \quad A_v = -\frac{R_f}{R_{in}}
\]
Output is inverted, gain magnitude can be less than, equal to, or greater than 1, and input impedance is just \(R_{in}\) — much lower than the non-inverting case, and worth checking against the source’s own output impedance.

title: Op-amp basics and example circuits
text:
Voltage follower (buffer)
The extreme case of the non-inverting amp: \(R_f = 0\), \(R_{in} = \infty\) (output tied directly to the inverting input, nothing else). Gain is exactly 1. Its entire purpose is impedance transformation — take a signal from a high-impedance, easily-loaded source and re-present it with the op-amp’s low output impedance, driving whatever comes next without disturbing the original signal.

title: Op-amp basics and example circuits
text:
Summing amplifier
An inverting amplifier with multiple input resistors into the same virtual-ground node. By superposition:
\[
V_{out} = -R_f\left(\frac{V_1}{R_1} + \frac{V_2}{R_2} + \cdots\right)
\]
Each input is weighted independently by its own resistor — the basis of analog audio mixers and resistor-ladder DACs.

title: Op-amp basics and example circuits
text:
Difference amplifier
Two inputs, four resistors: \(V_1\) through \(R_{in}\) into the inverting node (with \(R_f\) feedback, as usual), \(V_2\) through a matched \(R_{in}\) into the non-inverting node (with a matched \(R_f\) to ground, setting up a divider). With all four resistors matched in ratio:
\[
V_{out} = \frac{R_f}{R_{in}}(V_2 - V_1)
\]
Resistor matching here isn’t just a nicety — mismatch directly degrades common-mode rejection, letting noise that’s identical on both inputs leak into the output instead of canceling. (An instrumentation amplifier IC solves this properly with laser-trimmed internal resistors and a buffered front end; this discrete version is the conceptual starting point.)

title: Op-amp basics and example circuits
text:
Calculator: inverting / non-inverting gain



Where that 20 × log10 comes from is its own topic — see Gain and decibels.

title: Gain and decibels
text: Gain is just a ratio: output over input. A “gain of 11” means the output is 11 times the input — nothing more complicated than that. Decibels describe the exact same ratio on a logarithmic scale, and the reason that scale exists (and why it has two different-looking formulas) is worth actually deriving once rather than just memorizing.

title: Gain and decibels
text:
Where the decibel comes from
The unit originates with power ratios, from telephone engineering (the “Bel,” after Alexander Graham Bell, with “deci-” meaning a tenth of one):
\[
\text{dB} = 10 \log_{10}\left(\frac{P_2}{P_1}\right)
\]
That’s the fundamental definition. Everything else — including the \(20\log_{10}\) used for voltage and current — is derived from this one.

title: Gain and decibels
text:
Deriving the 20log(x) form
Power dissipated in a resistance is \(P = V^2/R\). If we’re comparing a voltage ratio across equal impedances (same \(R\) on both sides), the power ratio is the square of the voltage ratio:
\[
\frac{P_2}{P_1} = \frac{V_2^2/R}{V_1^2/R} = \left(\frac{V_2}{V_1}\right)^2
\]
Substituting into the power dB formula and pulling the exponent out of the log (since \(\log(x^2) = 2\log(x)\)):
\[
\text{dB} = 10 \log_{10}\left(\frac{V_2}{V_1}\right)^2 = 10 \times 2 \times \log_{10}\left(\frac{V_2}{V_1}\right) = 20 \log_{10}\left(\frac{V_2}{V_1}\right)
\]
The 20 isn’t a different unit or a different rule — it’s just the 10 from the original power definition, times the 2 that came out of squaring the voltage ratio. Same logic gives \(20\log_{10}(I_2/I_1)\) for current, since power also goes as \(I^2R\).
One honest caveat: that derivation assumed matched impedance on both sides of the ratio, which is exactly true for e.g. a coaxial cable’s attenuation and rarely exactly true for an op-amp stage’s voltage gain. In practice, \(20\log_{10}(\text{ratio})\) is used as the definition of a voltage or amplitude ratio in dB regardless of impedance matching — worth knowing where it historically comes from, without expecting a literal power interpretation from every voltage-gain dB figure you see on a datasheet.

The “−3 dB point” people constantly refer to (a filter’s cutoff, an amplifier’s bandwidth limit) is exactly the half-power point: \(10\log_{10}(0.5) = -3.01\,\text{dB}\), which corresponds to a voltage ratio of \(1/\sqrt{2} \approx 0.707\).

title: Gain and decibels
section: Why bother with logarithms at all
text:
Why bother with logarithms at all
Two practical reasons, beyond compressing huge ranges (a 120 dB op-amp open-loop gain is a ratio of 1,000,000 — far easier to write and reason about as “120 dB”):
Cascaded stages add instead of multiply. Three amplifier stages with gains of ×10, ×5, and ×2 multiply to ×100 in linear terms — but in dB, that’s 20 + 13.98 + 6.02 = 40 dB, a straight sum. For a signal chain with several stages, tracking dB and adding is far less error-prone than multiplying ratios by hand.
It matches how hearing works. The original motivation was audio — perceived loudness is roughly logarithmic in acoustic power, which is a large part of why dB became the standard unit for audio levels specifically, and then spread to RF and general electronics from there.

title: CAN
text: Controller Area Network was built for automotive wiring harnesses: many nodes on one twisted pair, no central controller, and a message-based model where nodes don’t address each other directly — a message just carries an identifier, and every node decides for itself whether to care.

title: CAN
text:
Differential signaling and arbitration
Like RS-485, CAN_H and CAN_L carry the same signal as a voltage difference, giving it the same noise-immunity advantage over long, electrically noisy cable runs (an engine bay is about as hostile an EMI environment as automotive electronics gets). Idle/recessive is both lines near the same voltage (~2.5 V, near-zero differential); a dominant bit pulls them apart.
That dominant/recessive asymmetry is what makes CAN’s arbitration work without a bus master: if multiple nodes start transmitting at the same time, they all monitor the bus while sending their identifier bit by bit. A node sending a recessive bit while it reads back a dominant one on the bus knows it lost arbitration — someone else’s frame has a lower (higher-priority) ID — and it silently backs off. The bus never collides in the way, say, early Ethernet could; the highest-priority message simply wins and keeps going.

title: CAN
text:
Bit timing
A CAN bit is divided into time quanta — sync segment, propagation segment, phase segment 1, phase segment 2 — configured in the controller’s bit timing registers as a prescaler and quanta-per-segment count. The resulting bit rate:
\[
f_{bit} = \frac{f_{clk}}{\text{BRP} \times (1 + T_{SEG1} + T_{SEG2})}
\]



Sample point (where in the bit the receiver actually latches the value) is normally targeted around 75–87.5% — check that number after changing segment values, not just the bit rate, since a bad sample point causes intermittent errors that only show up under specific bus loading or temperature.

title: CAN
text:
Implementing it in circuit
120 Ω termination at both physical ends of the bus, and only the ends. Same rule as RS-485, for the same reason — CAN is a linear bus topology, and unterminated or over-terminated ends cause reflections. A dedicated CAN transceiver IC (the TJA1050/TJA1051 family and equivalents are common) handles the differential drive; it is not something to attempt directly off microcontroller pins.
Keep stubs short. Branches off the main bus to reach a connector or node should be as short as practical (centimeters, not meters) — long stubs create their own reflections independent of the main bus termination.
Common-mode range and ground. CAN is differential, but it’s not immune to ground offset between nodes — the transceiver has a limited common-mode voltage range it can tolerate, and in installations spanning different power domains or long cable runs, that’s worth checking against the transceiver’s datasheet rather than assuming differential signaling makes ground irrelevant.
Isolation is common in industrial designs. Where a CAN node needs to survive a fault on the bus without taking the rest of the board down with it, an isolated CAN transceiver (or a non-isolated transceiver behind an isolated DC-DC and digital isolator) is the standard approach — automotive designs usually skip this since the whole vehicle shares one ground and power system, but industrial and multi-enclosure setups often can’t.

title: I2C
text: Two wires — SDA (data) and SCL (clock) — shared by every device on the bus, each identified by a 7-bit (or 10-bit) address. The mechanism that makes multi-drop work with just two wires is the open-drain output: every device can only pull a line low or let it float, never drive it high, so external pull-up resistors do the work of returning the line to logic 1.

title: I2C
section: Why open-drain, and why it matters for the pull-ups
text:
Why open-drain, and why it matters for the pull-ups
Because no device actively drives a “1,” two devices can pull the same line low at the same time without a conflict (whichever wants it low, wins) — this is what lets multiple masters share a bus and detect collisions safely, and what lets a slave “clock stretch” (hold SCL low) to pause a master mid-transaction. The cost is that the bus relies entirely on the pull-up resistors to define the high state and to charge the bus capacitance back up to a valid “1” — which is a genuine RC time constant problem, and it’s the actual constraint on how fast and how long an I2C bus can be.

title: I2C
text:
Sizing the pull-up resistors
Two competing limits set the valid range. Too small a resistor and a device can’t pull the line low enough (violating \(V_{OL}\)) or draws excess current; too large a resistor and the bus capacitance can’t charge fast enough to meet the rise-time spec at the chosen clock speed.
\[
R_{p,min} = \frac{V_{DD} - V_{OL,max}}{I_{OL,max}}, \qquad R_{p,max} = \frac{t_r}{0.8473 \, C_b}
\]
\(I_{OL,max}\) and \(V_{OL,max}\) come from the weakest device’s datasheet (3 mA / 0.4 V is a common spec). \(t_r\) is the maximum allowed rise time for the chosen speed grade, and \(C_b\) is the total bus capacitance — every device, every centimeter of trace or cable, adds to it.



Pick something in the middle of the calculated range, not right at either edge. Lower resistance suits longer buses or faster clocks (more capacitance to charge, less time to do it); higher resistance suits a short, lightly loaded standard-mode (100 kHz) bus, where values around 2.2–4.7 kΩ at 3.3 V are common.

title: I2C
text:
Other things to think about
Mixed-voltage buses. A 5 V device and a 3.3 V device can’t share pull-ups to different rails safely — use a dedicated I2C level-shifter IC, or the simple two-MOSFET bidirectional level-shifting circuit, rather than pulling up to whichever voltage is more convenient.
Bus length is really a capacitance budget. The 400 pF total bus capacitance cap in the standard specification isn’t arbitrary — it’s what keeps rise time in check at the given pull-up range. Long traces or cables eat into that budget fast; an I2C bus that needs to run any real distance usually wants an active bus buffer/extender IC, not just bigger pull-ups.
Address conflicts. Two devices with the same fixed 7-bit address can’t coexist on one bus. Check datasheets before committing to a design with multiple copies of the same sensor — many parts have one or two address-select pins for exactly this reason, and if that’s not enough, an I2C mux chip is the usual fix.

title: I2S
text: A synchronous serial protocol built specifically for streaming digital audio between chips — a DAC, a codec, a digital microphone — where SPI’s lack of a defined sample-boundary concept becomes a real problem.

title: I2S
text:
The three lines
BCLK (bit clock, one pulse per audio bit), WS/LRCLK (word select, marks which channel — left or right — the current bits belong to), and SD (serial data, the audio samples themselves, MSB first). Unlike SPI there’s no separate chip-select; a single I2S link is inherently point-to-point, and WS itself doubles as the frame marker.

title: I2S
text:
Clock relationship
The three clocks aren’t independent — BCLK, word select, and the underlying sample rate are tied together by the audio format itself:
\[
f_{BCLK} = f_s \times \text{bits per sample} \times \text{channels}
\]
Get this wrong (mismatched bit depth or channel count between transmitter and receiver) and audio still often “plays,” just pitched wrong or with channels swapped — a quieter failure mode than a digital bus simply not working.

title: I2S
text: Calculator: bit clock frequency

title: I2S
text:
Implementing it in circuit
Clock quality matters more here than on most digital buses. Jitter on BCLK or the master clock feeding it translates directly into audible noise in the analog output — this is the one protocol on this page where the purely digital signal’s timing precision has a straight line to perceived audio quality. A clean, low-jitter clock source is worth the extra cost on anything beyond a quick prototype.
Keep it away from switching noise and analog sections. Route I2S digital lines clear of switching regulators and any sensitive analog audio circuitry, and give the audio codec its own quiet ground/power area where board layout allows — digital switching noise coupling into an analog output stage is a classic source of audible whine or hiss.
It’s a short-range, intra-board (or short-cable) protocol as specified. Raw I2S isn’t designed for long cable runs the way S/PDIF or AES3 are — if audio needs to travel any real distance, convert to one of those standards rather than extending raw I2S.

title: Thyristors (SCR / TRIAC)
text: A thyristor is a four-layer PNPN device that behaves like nothing else on this page: it latches. A gate pulse triggers it into conduction, and it then stays conducting — no continued gate drive needed — until the main current drops below a minimum holding current \(I_H\), at which point it turns off on its own.

title: Thyristors (SCR / TRIAC)
text:
Silicon-controlled rectifier (SCR)
The basic thyristor: conducts in one direction only, like a diode, but stays off even when forward biased until the gate receives a trigger pulse. Once triggered and above \(I_H\), the gate loses all further control — the only way to turn it off is to bring the main current below \(I_H\), which in an AC circuit happens automatically every half-cycle as the waveform crosses zero.
That zero-crossing turn-off is exactly what makes SCRs useful for phase-controlled AC power delivery: triggering the gate at a chosen delay (firing angle \(\alpha\)) after each zero crossing controls how much of each half-cycle actually reaches the load, and the device turns itself off cleanly at the next crossing regardless.

Phase control and RMS output
For a resistive load, delaying the firing angle \(\alpha\) (0 to \(\pi\) radians within each half-cycle) reduces the RMS voltage delivered to the load:
\[
V_{RMS} = V_{in,RMS}\sqrt{1 - \frac{\alpha}{\pi} + \frac{\sin(2\alpha)}{2\pi}}
\]
\(\alpha = 0\) delivers the full waveform; \(\alpha = \pi\) delivers none. This is the mechanism behind old-style incandescent light dimmers.

title: Thyristors (SCR / TRIAC)
text:
TRIAC
An SCR only conducts one direction, so it only controls one half of an AC waveform. A TRIAC is functionally two SCRs wired anti-parallel in a single package, controllable from a single gate — it conducts (and can be triggered) on both half-cycles, which is why it’s the part actually found in most household dimmers and AC motor speed controls rather than a pair of discrete SCRs.

title: Thyristors (SCR / TRIAC)
text:
A caution worth stating plainly
Thyristor circuits usually work directly with mains voltage. That combination of high voltage and latching behavior (a triggered device won’t turn off just because the gate signal goes away) is genuinely dangerous to prototype casually — isolation, proper fusing, and mains-rated components matter here more than almost anywhere else on this site.

title: Bipolar junction transistors (BJT)
text: Two back-to-back PN junctions sharing a thin middle layer. A small current into the base controls a much larger current between collector and emitter — the mechanism behind both analog amplification and simple switching.

title: Bipolar junction transistors (BJT)
text:
NPN vs. PNP
NPN: emitter and collector are N-type, base is a thin P-type layer; current flows collector-to-emitter, conventional base current flows in. PNP is the mirror image — emitter/collector P-type, base N-type, currents reversed. NPN is more common in modern designs since electrons (the majority carrier doing the work in an NPN) have higher mobility than holes, giving better high-frequency performance for a given geometry.

title: Bipolar junction transistors (BJT)
text:
Current relationships
\[
I_C = \beta I_B, \qquad I_E = I_C + I_B
\]
\(\beta\) (also written \(h_{FE}\)) is typically 100–300 for small-signal parts, but varies significantly with temperature, collector current, and from device to device even within the same part number — never design something that depends on a precise \(\beta\) value.

title: Bipolar junction transistors (BJT)
text:
Operating regions

Cutoff: \(V_{BE}\) below ~0.6 V, no base current, transistor is off.
Active: base-emitter junction forward biased, base-collector junction reverse biased. \(I_C \approx \beta I_B\), roughly independent of \(V_{CE}\) (the slight upward slope in the figure is the Early effect). This is the amplifier region.
Saturation: both junctions forward biased, \(V_{CE}\) drops to a small value (~0.1–0.3 V), \(I_C\) is limited by the external circuit rather than \(\beta I_B\). This is the “fully on” switch region.

title: Bipolar junction transistors (BJT)
text:
Calculator: voltage-divider bias point
The standard way to bias an NPN in the active region: a resistor divider sets a stable base voltage, an emitter resistor stabilizes the operating point against \(\beta\) variation.
\[
V_B = V_{CC}\frac{R_2}{R_1+R_2}, \qquad I_E \approx \frac{V_B - 0.7}{R_E}, \qquad V_{CE} = V_{CC} - I_C(R_C+R_E)
\]



If \(V_{CE}\) comes out near 0 or negative, the resistor values are driving the transistor into saturation rather than the active region — reduce \(R_C\)/\(R_E\) or the base voltage.

title: Bipolar junction transistors (BJT)
text:
As a switch
Used as a switch, the goal is deliberately deep saturation rather than a well-controlled active-region current. Choosing enough base current to guarantee saturation across the worst-case (minimum) \(\beta\), with margin — a “forced \(\beta\)” of 10 rather than the datasheet’s typical 100–300 is a common conservative choice:
\[
I_{B} = \frac{I_{C}}{\beta_{forced}}, \qquad R_B = \frac{V_{in} - 0.7}{I_B}
\]

title: MOSFETs
text: A voltage on an insulated gate creates (or removes) a conductive channel between source and drain — no gate current flows in steady state, which is the main practical difference from a BJT’s current-controlled base.

title: MOSFETs
section: Enhancement vs. depletion, N vs. P channel
text:
Enhancement vs. depletion, N vs. P channel
Enhancement-mode devices (the vast majority in use today) are off at \(V_{GS}=0\) and need gate voltage past a threshold to turn on — safer as a default state, which is why they dominate. Depletion-mode devices are on at \(V_{GS}=0\) and need gate voltage to turn off. N-channel conducts with electrons and needs positive \(V_{GS}\); P-channel conducts with holes and needs negative \(V_{GS}\). N-channel is preferred where possible — electron mobility gives lower on-resistance for the same die area.

title: MOSFETs
text:
Regions of operation
Let \(V_{ov} = V_{GS} - V_{th}\) (the “overdrive” voltage). Using the simple square-law model:

Cutoff: \(V_{GS} < V_{th}\), no channel, \(I_D = 0\).
Triode / linear: \(V_{DS} < V_{ov}\), behaves like a voltage-controlled resistor: \(I_D = k\left(V_{ov}V_{DS} - \frac{V_{DS}^2}{2}\right)\)
Saturation: \(V_{DS} \geq V_{ov}\), current roughly flat (ideally independent of \(V_{DS}\)): \(I_D \approx \frac{k}{2}V_{ov}^2\)

Power MOSFETs are almost always operated either fully in triode (as a low-resistance switch) or fully off — the region in between is where switching loss happens, and a well-designed switching circuit spends as little time there as possible.

title: MOSFETs
text:
On-resistance and conduction loss
For a MOSFET used as a switch, the datasheet parameter that matters most is \(R_{DS(on)}\) — resistance while fully on. Conduction power loss follows directly:
\[
P_{cond} = I_{RMS}^2 \cdot R_{DS(on)}
\]
\(R_{DS(on)}\) rises with temperature (typically 30–50% higher at 125°C than at 25°C) and with gate drive that’s lower than the datasheet test condition — both worth checking against the datasheet curves, not just the headline number.

title: MOSFETs
text:
Calculator: conduction loss



Switching loss — the energy lost transitioning through the linear region on every turn-on/turn-off — depends on gate charge \(Q_g\), drive strength, and switching frequency, and generally dominates conduction loss at higher frequencies. Worth its own page once it’s next in the queue.

title: Diodes
text:
A diode is a single junction between P-type material (doped with acceptor atoms, majority carriers are holes) and N-type material (doped with donor atoms, majority carriers are electrons). Where they meet, carriers diffuse across and recombine, leaving behind a region stripped of free carriers — the depletion region — with a built-in electric field opposing further diffusion.
Forward bias (P side positive relative to N) narrows the depletion region and, past a threshold, lets current flow easily. Reverse bias widens it and current stays near zero — until reverse breakdown.



Fig. 1 — diode symbol, and current vs. voltage for both bias directions.

title: Diodes
text:
A diode is a single junction between P-type material (doped with acceptor atoms, majority carriers are holes) and N-type material (doped with donor atoms, majority carriers are electrons). Where they meet, carriers diffuse across and recombine, leaving behind a region stripped of free carriers — the depletion region — with a built-in electric field opposing further diffusion.
Forward bias (P side positive relative to N) narrows the depletion region and, past a threshold, lets current flow easily. Reverse bias widens it and current stays near zero — until reverse breakdown.



Fig. 1 — diode symbol, and current vs. voltage for both bias directions.

title: Diodes
text:
The diode equation
\[
I = I_S \left( e^{V / (nV_T)} - 1 \right)
\]
\(I_S\) is the reverse saturation current (tiny, often pA–nA), \(n\) is the ideality factor (close to 1 for a good diode), and \(V_T = kT/q \approx 25.85\,\text{mV}\) at room temperature. The exponential is why forward voltage looks almost like a fixed ~0.6–0.7 V (silicon) rather than a smooth ramp — current changes by roughly 10× for every ~60 mV of forward voltage.
Forward voltage drops slightly with temperature, about \(-2\,\text{mV/°C}\) for silicon — worth remembering when a design runs hot.

title: Diodes
text:
Rectification
A single diode passes only one half of an AC waveform (half-wave rectification). Four diodes in a bridge pass both halves in the same direction (full-wave), roughly doubling the ripple frequency seen by the output filter capacitor and halving the required capacitance for the same ripple — the same \(C = \Delta I / (f \cdot \Delta V)\) relationship as the buck converter’s output cap, just driven by load current instead of inductor ripple current.

title: Diodes
section: Calculator: series resistor for a diode or LED
text:
Calculator: series resistor for a diode or LED
The most common practical use of the diode equation: given a supply and a target forward current, size the series resistor. Treats the diode’s forward drop as roughly constant, which is accurate enough for design work once \(V_f\) is known from a datasheet.
\[
R = \frac{V_{supply} - V_f}{I_f}
\]

title: Zener and Schottky diodes
text: Two diode variants built around a normal PN junction’s least-wanted properties — breakdown and switching delay — turned into features.

title: Zener and Schottky diodes
text:
Zener diodes
A standard diode’s reverse breakdown is destructive if the current isn’t limited — but a Zener is doped specifically to break down at a well-controlled voltage \(V_Z\) and survive it indefinitely, provided power dissipation stays within its rating. That gives a cheap, if imprecise (a few percent, and temperature-sensitive), voltage reference.

Basic shunt regulator
A series resistor from the supply into the Zener (with the load in parallel) sets the Zener current; the resistor must be sized so the Zener always sees at least its minimum regulation current, across the full load current range:
\[
R = \frac{V_{in} - V_Z}{I_Z + I_{load}}
\]
Simple and lossy — the series resistor burns power continuously, and regulation is only as good as the Zener’s own impedance. Fine for a low-current reference or bias supply, not for anything power-hungry (a linear or switching regulator does the same job far more efficiently).


Calculator

title: Zener and Schottky diodes
text:
Schottky diodes
A Schottky diode replaces the PN junction with a metal-semiconductor junction. Two practical consequences follow directly from that:
Lower forward voltage — typically 0.2–0.4 V versus 0.6–0.7 V for silicon PN — because there’s no minority-carrier injection barrier to overcome in the same way.
No reverse-recovery time — a PN diode stores minority charge while conducting and takes tens to hundreds of nanoseconds to stop conducting when reverse-biased; a Schottky is a majority-carrier device with essentially none of that, so it switches off almost instantly.
That combination is exactly why Schottkys show up as the freewheeling/catch diode in unsynchronized buck converters and as reverse-polarity protection where the forward drop matters. The trade-offs: higher reverse leakage current (worse with temperature) and generally lower reverse voltage ratings than comparable PN diodes.

title: SPI
text: Four wires, one shared clock, full duplex, and no addressing scheme at all — the master picks which device it’s talking to by which chip-select (CS) line it pulls low. That simplicity is why SPI is usually the fastest option available for a given part.

title: SPI
text:
The four lines
MOSI (master out, slave in), MISO (master in, slave out), SCK (clock, always driven by the master), and CS/SS (chip select, one per slave device, active low by convention). Data shifts in and out simultaneously on every clock edge — full duplex is inherent to the protocol, not an add-on.

title: SPI
text:
Clock polarity and phase
Devices must agree on which clock edge data is sampled on — this is the CPOL/CPHA setting, usually written as “mode 0” through “mode 3”:

title: SPI
text:
Calculator: throughput



Ignores per-transaction overhead (CS setup/hold time, any gaps between bytes) — real throughput on a given MCU is usually somewhat lower, especially for many small transfers where that overhead repeats.

title: SPI
text:
Implementing it in circuit
No arbitration, no error checking, so signal integrity is entirely on you. Unlike I2C or CAN, nothing in the protocol itself detects a corrupted bit — a marginal signal just produces wrong data with no indication anything went wrong. That makes trace length and clock speed a real trade-off: fine at a few MHz over several centimeters of board trace, but pushing tens of MHz over more than a few centimeters (or any real cable) risks reflections without proper termination or controlled impedance traces.
Every device needs its own CS line. Fan-out gets expensive fast — five SPI slaves means five CS pins from the master, even though MOSI/MISO/SCK are shared. Some parts support “daisy-chaining” (each device forwards data to the next), which trades pin count for more complex framing.
Series termination resistors (typically 22–33 Ω, placed close to the driving pin) are a cheap, common fix for ringing on SCK or MOSI when trace lengths get long relative to the clock’s rise time — worth having as an option in the layout even if unpopulated on the first spin.
Keep clock and data lines length-matched at higher speeds, and away from noisy switching signals (like a nearby buck converter’s switch node) — SPI has no error correction to fall back on if coupled noise corrupts a bit.

title: RS-232 and RS-485
text: Both are electrical standards for carrying UART-style framed data over a cable — neither defines the byte framing itself (that’s still start/data/parity/stop bits, as on the UART page). What they define is how the 1s and 0s are represented as voltages on the wire, and that choice determines cable length, noise immunity, and whether more than two devices can share a bus.

title: RS-232 and RS-485
text:
RS-232: single-ended, point-to-point
Logic levels are inverted and much larger than TTL: a valid “1” (mark) is −3 V to −15 V, a valid “0” (space) is +3 V to +15 V, with ±5 V to ±12 V the common real-world range. That wide swing is why it can’t come straight off a microcontroller pin — it needs a dedicated line driver/receiver chip (the MAX232 family is the classic choice) to convert between TTL and RS-232 levels, generating the negative supply internally from charge-pump capacitors.
Point-to-point only — one transmitter, one receiver, traditionally a DB9 connector. Reliable to roughly 15 m / 50 ft at modest baud rates; longer runs need RS-422 or RS-485 instead.

title: RS-232 and RS-485
text:
RS-485: differential, multi-drop
Instead of one signal wire referenced to ground, RS-485 uses a twisted pair (A/B, sometimes called D+/D−) carrying the same signal as a voltage difference between the two wires. Noise picked up by the cable tends to hit both wires equally and cancels out at the differential receiver — this is why RS-485 tolerates much longer cable runs and noisier environments than single-ended RS-232 or TTL.
Multiple transmitters and receivers can share one bus (up to 32 standard-load devices, more with modern reduced-load transceivers), which is why it’s the usual choice for a chain of sensors or a Modbus network. Since UART itself has no arbitration, RS-485 multi-drop networks need a protocol layer above it (like Modbus) to make sure only one device drives the bus at a time.

Termination and biasing — the part people get wrong
Two things a working RS-485 bus needs that a point-to-point link doesn’t:
120 Ω termination resistors at both physical ends of the bus (matching the cable’s characteristic impedance), and nowhere in between. Terminating every node, or terminating only one end, causes reflections that corrupt data at higher baud rates or longer cable lengths.
Fail-safe biasing — a pull-up on the A line and a pull-down on the B line (typically 560 Ω–650 Ω, sized with the termination resistors to keep the idle differential voltage above the receiver’s threshold, around 200 mV) so the bus reads a defined idle state when no device is actively driving it. Without this, an idle bus can float into the undefined region between logic states and receivers may see noise as random bit errors. Some transceiver ICs include this internally; many don’t.
Distance and speed trade off directly: roughly 10 Mbps at a few meters down to about 100 kbps at 1200 m, per the standard’s typical guidance — check the specific transceiver’s datasheet for its real numbers.

title: UART
text: A Universal Asynchronous Receiver/Transmitter sends bytes with no shared clock line — timing is agreed in advance (the baud rate) and each byte is framed with start/stop bits so the receiver can find the edges on its own.

title: UART
text:
Framing
Idle line sits high. A frame is: one start bit (line pulled low), 5–9 data bits (LSB first), an optional parity bit, then one or more stop bits (line released high):
\[
\text{frame bits} = 1 + \text{data bits} + [\text{parity?} 1 : 0] + \text{stop bits}
\]
Both ends must agree on baud rate, data bits, parity, and stop bits beforehand — there’s no negotiation. Get any of the four wrong and you get garbage or nothing.

title: UART
section: Calculator: bit time and frame time
text: Calculator: bit time and frame time

title: UART
text:
Implementing it in circuit
Voltage levels first. A microcontroller’s UART pins swing between 0 V and its logic supply (3.3 V or 5 V) — that’s TTL/CMOS-level UART, not RS-232 (see the next page). Connecting a 5 V UART TX directly into a 3.3 V-only RX pin can overstress the input; check the receiving device’s absolute maximum, and add a level shifter or a simple resistor divider if there’s any doubt.
TX goes to RX. Obvious once stated, a common wiring mistake otherwise — device A’s TX connects to device B’s RX, and vice versa. Boards labeled from the device’s own perspective (a USB-serial adapter’s “TX” is what it transmits) make this easy to get backwards.
Common ground is mandatory. UART is single-ended — the receiver decides high/low relative to its own ground pin. If the two devices don’t share a ground reference (separate power supplies, long cable runs), add a ground wire alongside the signal wires, or use an isolated UART transceiver if the two sides genuinely need to float independently.
Cable length and speed trade off. Bare TTL-level UART over an unshielded wire is only reliable for short runs (tens of centimeters to maybe a meter, more at lower baud rates) before ringing and noise pickup cause errors — for anything longer, convert to RS-232 or RS-485 at the electrical layer instead of pushing raw TTL levels down a long cable.

title: Op-amp frequency response
text: The gain formulas on the op-amp basics page — \(1 + R_f/R_{in}\), \(-R_f/R_{in}\) — assume an ideal op-amp with infinite, frequency-independent open-loop gain. Real ones don’t have that, and the way they fall short shapes both how much bandwidth you actually get and whether the circuit stays stable at all.

title: Op-amp frequency response
text:
Open-loop gain isn’t flat
A real op-amp’s open-loop gain is enormous at DC (typically 100 dB to 120 dB — a ratio of 100,000 to 1,000,000) but starts rolling off at a surprisingly low frequency, often just single-digit to tens of Hz. That’s deliberate: op-amps are internally frequency-compensated with a dominant pole specifically to keep the response falling at a predictable, well-behaved −20 dB/decade past that corner, all the way out to where the gain reaches unity (0 dB).

title: Op-amp frequency response
text:
Gain-bandwidth product
Past the dominant pole’s corner frequency, gain falls off as \(1/f\) — which means gain times frequency is constant. That constant is the gain-bandwidth product (GBW), a single number on every op-amp datasheet:
\[
GBW = A_{open-loop} \times f_{corner} = A_{closed-loop} \times f_{-3dB, closed-loop}
\]
Both sides of that equation describe the same straight line on a log-log plot — one point on it is the open-loop DC gain and its corner frequency; every other point is some closed-loop gain and the bandwidth it gets. Rearranged into the form actually used when picking resistor values:
\[
f_{-3dB} \approx \frac{GBW}{A_{noise\ gain}}
\]
“Noise gain” here means \(1 + R_f/R_{in}\) in both the inverting and non-inverting configurations — for the inverting amp specifically, that’s not the same as its signal gain (\(-R_f/R_{in}\)); the feedback network sets bandwidth according to the noise gain regardless of which input the signal actually enters.

title: Op-amp frequency response
text:
Calculator: closed-loop bandwidth



More gain always costs bandwidth, in direct proportion — a 10 MHz GBW part gives roughly 1 MHz of bandwidth at a noise gain of 10, or 100 kHz at a noise gain of 100. If a design needs both high gain and wide bandwidth, that’s usually solved with multiple lower-gain stages in series rather than one stage doing it all, since bandwidth divides by the product of per-stage gains but each stage individually only pays for its own gain.

title: Op-amp frequency response
text:
Phase lag and phase margin
Every pole in a system contributes phase lag that reaches 45° right at its corner frequency and approaches a full 90° well above it. A single dominant pole — most of an op-amp’s usable range — contributes phase approaching −90°. Real op-amps have additional (higher-frequency) poles from other internal stages, which add further phase lag as frequency climbs toward and past the unity-gain frequency.
This matters because of how the feedback loop actually behaves: if the total phase lag around the loop reaches a full 180° at the frequency where loop gain is still 1 (0 dB), the negative feedback the whole circuit depends on effectively becomes positive feedback — the circuit oscillates instead of amplifying.
Phase margin is the safety cushion against that: 180° minus the total phase lag, measured at the frequency where loop gain crosses 0 dB. A single dominant pole alone gives close to 90° of margin (comfortably stable); each additional pole below the crossover frequency eats into it. Common design targets:

≥ 45° phase margin — generally considered the minimum for acceptable behavior.
~60–65° phase margin — a common sweet spot: well damped, minimal step-response overshoot, without sacrificing more bandwidth than necessary.
< 45° — increasing peaking in the frequency response and overshoot/ringing in the step response; margins approaching 0° mean sustained oscillation.

title: Op-amp frequency response
text:
Reading a Bode plot
The standard way this all gets presented: two stacked plots sharing a log-frequency x-axis. The magnitude plot (dB vs. frequency) shows straight-line segments — flat, then breaking downward by 20 dB/decade at each pole’s corner. The phase plot (degrees vs. frequency) shows each pole’s transition, passing through −45° at its own corner and flattening out near −90° roughly a decade above it. Reading both together at the loop’s unity-gain crossover point is exactly how phase margin gets checked, whether by hand from a datasheet graph or automatically in simulation.

title: Tools
text:
Small browser-based utilities that talk directly to hardware over USB — no app to install, no drivers beyond what your OS already has for a USB-serial adapter.

These use the Web Serial API, which currently only works in Chrome, Edge, or another Chromium-based browser on desktop, over HTTPS. It will not work in Firefox, Safari, or any mobile browser — the page will tell you if your browser isn't supported.


Serial monitor — connect to a serial device, watch incoming data live, send lines back.
Serial file sender — send a file as raw bytes over a serial connection, with a progress bar. Useful for simple UART bootloaders that expect a raw byte stream; it does not implement chip-specific flashing protocols (STK500, DFU, and similar).

title: LC and RC filter design
text: The two filters you reach for constantly: a simple RC low-pass for signal-level filtering, and an LC low-pass for power-stage or EMI filtering where you can’t afford a resistor’s power loss.

title: LC and RC filter design
text:
RC low-pass
A single resistor and capacitor to ground give a first-order (−20 dB/decade) low-pass with cutoff:
\[
f_c = \frac{1}{2\pi R C}
\]
Simple, but the resistor dissipates power continuously — fine for a signal line, not for filtering a DC-DC converter’s output current.

Calculator

title: LC and RC filter design
text:
LC low-pass
Replacing the resistor with an inductor removes the continuous power loss — the standard choice at a converter’s output or as an input EMI filter. Second-order (−40 dB/decade) response:
\[
f_c = \frac{1}{2\pi\sqrt{LC}}
\]
For a target cutoff, there’s a free parameter — usually chosen via the filter’s characteristic impedance \(Z_0 = \sqrt{L/C}\), which should roughly match the source/load impedance to avoid ringing:
\[
L = \frac{Z_0}{2\pi f_c}, \qquad C = \frac{1}{2\pi f_c Z_0}
\]
A too-low \(Z_0\) makes for a large capacitor and a peaky, underdamped response without added series resistance; too high makes for a large, lossy inductor. Real designs also check the \(Q\) at \(f_c\) against the source/load resistance and add damping if it rings.

title: Buck-boost converter
text: The classic (inverting) buck-boost can step the output above or below the input, at the cost of an inverted polarity — the output is referenced negative to the input’s ground. Same ideal CCM treatment as the buck and boost pages.

title: Buck-boost converter
text:
Duty cycle
\[
\frac{|V_{out}|}{V_{in}} = \frac{D}{1-D} \quad \Rightarrow \quad D = \frac{|V_{out}|}{V_{in} + |V_{out}|}
\]
\(D < 0.5\) steps down, \(D > 0.5\) steps up — the same switch duty cycle range covers both directions, which is the whole appeal of the topology.

title: Buck-boost converter
text:
Inductor current
The inductor is charged from \(V_{in}\) only, during the on-time — same charging behavior as a boost:
\[
\Delta I_L = \frac{V_{in} D}{f_{sw} L} \quad \Rightarrow \quad L = \frac{V_{in} D}{f_{sw}\, \Delta I_L}
\]
And the output only sees current during the off-time, so — again like a boost —
\[
I_{L,avg} = \frac{I_{out}}{1-D}
\]
This is the least efficient of the three topologies in practice: the inductor carries both the input and output current duty cycles, so RMS current (and core/copper loss) tends to be the highest of the three for a given output power.

title: About
text:
I’m a hardware engineer, and on any given day I might be reading about magnetics, debugging an IC datasheet, tuning a microcontroller peripheral, or writing the software that ties it all together. For a long time the notes from that ended up scattered across notebooks and apps on different devices, half-findable at best.
This site is where those notes live now, split into three parts: a Notebook of topic write-ups with the math worked out, a set of browser-based Tools for the bench, and a Calculators section that pulls every calculator out of the notebook into one place for quick use without the derivation.
It’s a running project: chapters, tools, and calculators get added as I work through new topics, and existing notes get revised as I learn more or find a cleaner way to derive something.

title: Series and parallel resistance
text:
Resistors in series share the same current, and their voltage drops add — so resistance simply sums:
\[
R_{series} = R_1 + R_2 + R_3
\]

title: Series and parallel resistance
text:
Resistors in series share the same current, and their voltage drops add — so resistance simply sums:
\[
R_{series} = R_1 + R_2 + R_3
\]

title: Series and parallel resistance
text:
Parallel
Resistors in parallel share the same voltage, and their currents add, giving a reciprocal sum:
\[
\frac{1}{R_{parallel}} = \frac{1}{R_1} + \frac{1}{R_2} + \frac{1}{R_3}
\]
The parallel combination is always smaller than the smallest individual resistor — adding a path for current can only make it easier for current to flow.

title: Impedance of R, L, C
text:
A resistor’s impedance is frequency-independent. An inductor and capacitor’s impedances are imaginary and move in opposite directions with frequency:
\[
Z_R = R, \qquad Z_L = j\omega L, \qquad Z_C = \frac{1}{j\omega C}
\]
with \(\omega = 2\pi f\). Their magnitudes — reactance — are what you actually size components against:
\[
X_L = \omega L = 2\pi f L, \qquad X_C = \frac{1}{\omega C} = \frac{1}{2\pi f C}
\]
\(X_L\) grows with frequency (an inductor looks like an open circuit at high frequency); \(X_C\) shrinks with frequency (a capacitor looks like a short at high frequency).

title: Impedance of R, L, C
text:
A resistor’s impedance is frequency-independent. An inductor and capacitor’s impedances are imaginary and move in opposite directions with frequency:
\[
Z_R = R, \qquad Z_L = j\omega L, \qquad Z_C = \frac{1}{j\omega C}
\]
with \(\omega = 2\pi f\). Their magnitudes — reactance — are what you actually size components against:
\[
X_L = \omega L = 2\pi f L, \qquad X_C = \frac{1}{\omega C} = \frac{1}{2\pi f C}
\]
\(X_L\) grows with frequency (an inductor looks like an open circuit at high frequency); \(X_C\) shrinks with frequency (a capacitor looks like a short at high frequency).

title: Impedance of R, L, C
text:
Series RLC magnitude
For R, L, and C in series, the reactances subtract (they’re 180° apart) before combining with resistance:
\[
|Z| = \sqrt{R^2 + (X_L - X_C)^2}
\]
This hits a minimum, \(|Z| = R\), at the resonant frequency where \(X_L = X_C\).
